standard.title: Composite Bottom for Stainless Steel Cooking Utensils — Specification (सम्मिश्र तलें के स्टेनलेस स्टील के पकाने के बर्तन — विशिष्टि)
standard.sector: Mechanical Engineering / Utensils, Cutlery and Domestic Hardware

sectional_committee.name: Utensils, Cutlery and Domestic Hardware Sectional Committee

standard.description: This standard prescribes the requirements for materials, design, manufacture, dimensional limits, and physical-thermal testing of composite bottoms (sandwich, clad, or encapsulated designs) of stainless steel cooking utensils to ensure high thermal conductivity, rapid heat distribution, and durable joint adhesion.
standard.scope: This standard prescribes the requirements for materials, design, manufacture, dimensional limits, and physical-thermal testing of composite bottoms (sandwich, clad, or encapsulated designs) of stainless steel cooking utensils to ensure high thermal conductivity, rapid heat distribution, and durable joint adhesion.

supersedes: IS 4536 (Parts 1 to 3) (which historically covered copper electro-deposited
and copper-clad bottoms of stainless steel utensils)

certification.description: Voluntary Product Certification. However, under the Cookware and Utensils (Quality Control) Order 2024 issued by the Ministry of Commerce and Industry, Government of India, many categories of cookware are under mandatory BIS certification (effective 1 September 2024). This requires all composite-bottom stainless steel cookware manufactured or imported into India to carry the prestigious physical ISI 'Standard Mark' stamped on the steel body, certifying strict compliance with IS 15960.
requirements: Under the active Amendment No. 1 (June 2024), the stainless steel sheet used to manufacture the utensil body must conform to designations X07Cr18Ni9 or X04Cr19Ni9 of IS 5522 or IS 6911, or to grades N1, N2, or N3 of IS 15997.

Requires bonding high-purity, wrought aluminium (conforming to IS 21) or pure copper to the bottom of the stainless steel vessel. This utilizes the thermal conductivity of the inner core to eliminate localized 'hot spots' that cause food burning, while maintaining a hygienic steel cooking surface.

Bond strength is evaluated using a specialized drop-impact rig. A steel ball weighing exactly half a kilogram (500 g) is dropped from a vertical height of 500 mm (0.5 m) directly onto the center of the composite bottom.
Following repeated impact cycles of the 500g steel ball, the composite bottom must show zero cracking, peeling, joint separation, or visual delamination.

To simulate real-world dry-boiling, the utensil is dry-heated to a temperature of 250°C to 260°C and immediately quenched in cold water at ambient temperature, repeating this cycle for 25 consecutive times.
Following the 25 thermal shock dry-heat quench cycles, the composite base must show zero blisters, separations, peeling, or joint failures under physical inspection.
The finished utensil is degreased in acetone and submerged for 16 hours in boiling chemical solutions of 99% Glacial Acetic Acid and Sodium Chloride maintained at 60°C ± 2°C.
The stainless steel cooking surface must show zero signs of pitting, discoloration, rust staining, or localized corrosion following the 16-hour chemical exposure.

All observed or calculated test and analytical values (such as sheet thickness, impact heights, and temperatures) must be mathematically rounded off in accordance with IS 2:1960. The number of significant places retained should match that of the specified value in the standard.
